title: Jeremiah 40:7–16
context: Jeremiah 40:7–16 is told by the narrator and describes Gedaliah’s brief governorship at Mizpah. The captains of the forces still in the field hear that the king of Babylon has made Gedaliah governor, and they come to him with their men: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite (40:7–8). The shorter list in 2 Kings 25:23 names “Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite” and does not mention Jonathan or the sons of Ephai; the lists are named without harmonizing. Gedaliah swears to them that they should serve the king of Babylon and live (40:9–10; compare 2 Kings 25:24), a counsel that echoes Jeremiah’s own message (compare 21:9). Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon, Edom, and other lands return and gather a rich harvest (40:11–12). Johanan warns Gedaliah that Baalis king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael to kill him, and secretly offers to kill Ishmael first, but Gedaliah refuses to believe him and forbids it (40:13–16). The text does not explain Baalis’s reasons, and these notes do not supply them. Both traditions read the passage soberly: a fragile remnant is given a season of peace and harvest, while the threat the reader is warned of goes unheeded.

verses.text: Now when all the captains of the forces who were in the fields, even they and their men, heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam governor in the land, and had committed to him men, women, children, and of the poorest of the land, of those who were not carried away captive to Babylon,
verses.arminianNotes: The captains of the forces in the field heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor and had committed to him men, women, children, and the poorest of the land. Arminian readers note that Gedaliah’s appointment offered stability to those left behind and they see hope for a remnant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that 2 Kings 25:22–23 gives a shorter account of the appointment, named without harmonizing. They read the verse as showing a fragile new beginning among the remnant, with leaders gathering around the governor whom Babylon had appointed over the land.

verses.text: then Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, and Seraiah the son of Tanhumeth, and the sons of Ephai the Netophathite, and Jezaniah the son of the Maacathite, they and their men came to Gedaliah to Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes: Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, Johanan and Jonathan the sons of Kareah, Seraiah, the sons of Ephai, and Jezaniah came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. Arminian readers note that 2 Kings 25:23 names “Jaazaniah the son of the Maacathite” and does not mention Jonathan or the sons of Ephai, named without harmonizing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same differences between the lists and do not reconcile them. They observe that Ishmael and Johanan, both named here, will become central to what follows, and they read the gathering as a moment of potential unity that will soon be broken.

verses.text: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan swore to them and to their men, saying, “Don’t be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.
verses.arminianNotes: Gedaliah swore to them, “Don’t be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon, and it will be well with you.” Arminian readers note that this counsel echoes Jeremiah’s message (compare 21:9), and they see Gedaliah as urging a path of peace and survival.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the parallel in 2 Kings 25:24, named without harmonizing, and the agreement with Jeremiah’s counsel. They read Gedaliah’s oath as an effort to secure the remnant’s future through submission to Babylon, which the prophet had presented as the LORD’s will in that season.

verses.text: As for me, behold, I will dwell at Mizpah, to stand before the Chaldeans who will come to us; but you, gather wine and summer fruits and oil, and put them in your vessels, and dwell in your cities that you have taken.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gedaliah says he will dwell at Mizpah to stand before the Chaldeans, and tells the captains to gather wine, summer fruits, and oil and dwell in their cities. Arminian readers note that Gedaliah takes responsibility for dealing with Babylon so the people can rebuild their lives in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same arrangement and observe that the harvest of wine, fruit, and oil suggests a season of provision after the siege. They read the verse as a brief picture of ordinary life resuming, which both traditions see as a mercy within judgment.

verses.text: Likewise when all the Jews who were in Moab, and among the children of Ammon, and in Edom, and who were in all the countries, heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant of Judah, and that he had set over them Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan,
verses.arminianNotes: Jews in Moab, among the Ammonites, in Edom, and in other countries heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant and set Gedaliah over them. Arminian readers note that news of the remnant drew scattered people home, and they see hope that the community might be rebuilt in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the return of scattered Jews shows the significance of Gedaliah’s appointment for the wider community. They read the verse as part of a brief season of gathering that stands in contrast to the scattering described in the surrounding chapters.

verses.text: then all the Jews returned out of all places where they were driven, and came to the land of Judah, to Gedaliah, to Mizpah, and gathered very much wine and summer fruits.
verses.arminianNotes: All the Jews returned from where they had been driven, came to Gedaliah at Mizpah, and gathered very much wine and summer fruits. Arminian readers note the abundance of the harvest and see it as a sign of God’s kindness to a humbled people, even after the devastation of the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same abundance and read it as a mercy within judgment. They observe that the narrator’s mention of a plentiful harvest heightens the tragedy of what follows, since a season of peace and provision is soon interrupted by violence.

verses.text: Moreover Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were in the fields, came to Gedaliah to Mizpah,
verses.arminianNotes: Johanan the son of Kareah and all the captains of the forces came to Gedaliah at Mizpah. Arminian readers note that Johanan comes forward as a concerned leader, and they see him acting to protect the governor and the fragile community gathered around him at Mizpah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Johanan’s role grows in the following chapters, where he leads the remnant (41:11–18; 42:1). They read this verse as introducing his warning and observe that the captains come together, which suggests their concern was shared rather than private.

verses.text: and said to him, “Do you know that Baalis the king of the children of Ammon has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?” But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam didn’t believe them.
verses.arminianNotes: The captains asked, “Do you know that Baalis the king of the children of Ammon has sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to take your life?” But Gedaliah didn’t believe them. Arminian readers note the warning and Gedaliah’s refusal to believe it, and they read it without judging his motives.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the text does not explain why Baalis wanted Gedaliah dead, and they do not supply a reason. They observe that Gedaliah’s trust in Ishmael, though perhaps generous, left the remnant exposed, and they read the verse soberly as setting up the tragedy to come.

verses.text: Then Johanan the son of Kareah spoke to Gedaliah in Mizpah secretly, saying, “Please let me go, and I will kill Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and no man will know it. Why should he take your life, that all the Jews who are gathered to you should be scattered, and the remnant of Judah perish?”
verses.arminianNotes: Johanan secretly offered to kill Ishmael so that the remnant of Judah would not be scattered. Arminian readers note that Johanan’s concern for the remnant is real, while observing that his plan involves killing without judgment, which raises its own moral questions the text does not resolve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same tension between Johanan’s concern for the people and his proposal of a secret killing. They read the verse as part of the narrator’s realistic portrayal of a desperate situation, without endorsing Johanan’s plan or condemning his fear.

verses.text: But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam said to Johanan the son of Kareah, “You shall not do this thing, for you speak falsely of Ishmael.”
verses.arminianNotes: Gedaliah said to Johanan, “You shall not do this thing, for you speak falsely of Ishmael.” Arminian readers note that Gedaliah refuses to act on suspicion and to permit a killing, and they see in his response both integrity and a fatal misjudgment of Ishmael’s intentions.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gedaliah’s refusal is honorable in forbidding murder, even though his trust proves misplaced. They read the verse as a sober reminder that good intentions do not always guard against treachery, and they leave the evaluation of his judgment to the reader.
